newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Iran diplomats confirm trade ban on New Zealand.
newsitem.headline: Iran diplomats confirm trade ban on New Zealand.

text.p: Iran's embassy in New Zealand on Monday confirmed that Tehran had cut off trade relations with New Zealand in the latest round of a diplomatic row sparked by a German court ruling linking Iran to terrorism.
In a statement the embassy said Iran "...has ordered the suspension of all trade agreements with New Zealand parties until further notice".
It also confirmed that Tehran was recalling its ambassador to New Zealand, Mohammad Sazegara, from Tuesday.
The statement criticised New Zealand for departing from what it called "an independent position and vote" on international issues by joining international diplomatic action against Iran.

Wellington recalled its ambassador temporarily from Tehran on Friday as part of a coordinated response, led by European Union states, to a German court ruling that Iran had ordered the 1992 murders of four Kurdish dissidents in Berlin.
The next day Iran's official IRNA news agency said trade had been suspended, but New Zealand government officials tried to play this down on Monday, saying a ban had not been confirmed.
Speaking at a news conference before the embassy issued its statement, International Trade Minister Lockwood Smith said the ban report might have stemmed from "some misunderstanding".
But the Iranian diplomats left little doubt in their statement that the ban was directly linked to the recall of ambassador Daniel Richards.
It accused New Zealand of entering into "a political show against Iran" in its reaction to the German court decision.

Smith had also suggested to reporters that it was possible the ban followed an erroneous initial report about New Zealand's move on Friday that had suggested Wellington wanted to curb trade ties with Iran.
"New Zealand has never linked trade to these (political) issues," he said, emphasising that no such action was planned.
In its only conciliatory paragraph, the Iranian embassy statement referred to the prospect of dialogue to smooth over relations later this week.
Sazegara would seek to meet his New Zealand counterpart Richards in a few days' time, it said.
The two hoped "to meet and discuss with Iranian authorities...with a view to normalising the relations between both countries on the basis of mutual respect", it said.
Since the row broke out at the weekend, some of New Zealand's primary exporters have expressed concerns about the effects of a full-scale ban on their agricultural produce trade.

The trade, mainly in lamb, dairy produce and wool, is not on a large scale in overall terms -- totalling an estimated NZ$170 million ($119 million) last year -- but was big enough to cause short-term problems if suspended, producers said.

Asked about the possible financial impact of a trade dispute, Smith told reporters earlier on Monday: "That's not the point... We have always had good relations with Iran and we want to get them back on a good footing."
